walkthroughs.body_html:
Electrochemistry — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Electrochemistry brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Electrochemistry.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.
The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.

mcqs.q: What is different between two isotopes of the same element?
options: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes are atoms of different elements with the same mass.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Isotopes have different numbers of electrons, which is why their mass differs.
